## G. THE GREAT FLOOD (6:5–9:29)

### C-V1R4-01 | Flood cause: moral, extensive + intensive sin
- **Claim:** Hamilton reads 6:5 as establishing a clear moral motivation for the Flood: God never acts arbitrarily; judgment falls for deliberate violation of God’s will, not mere humanity. What God “saw” was both extensiveness and intensiveness of sin—every scheme of imagination evil *perpetually*.
- **Quote:** “The God of the OT never acts arbitrarily; he does not run his world amorally… Nobody will receive this divine judgment simply because he is human. … Here, first of all, is what God saw (v. 5), then how he felt (v. 6), then what he intends to do (v. 7). What God saw was both the extensiveness of sin and the intensiveness of sin.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 37–42; Gen 6:5
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[sin]], [[flood-universality]]

### C-V1R4-02 | Universal vs local: ʾereṣ / kol-hāʾāreṣ
- **Claim:** In 6:5–13 *hāʾāreṣ* appears eight times, looking like a universal condition. Hamilton notes ʾereṣ can mean local land, but when a particular land is meant it often has a further identifying phrase; *kol-hāʾāreṣ* (outside Deuteronomy and Joshua–Samuel) is usually “earth,” though Gen 13:9, 15 show it can mean whole land even in Genesis. He treats the Flood’s geographic claim as universal-leaning while acknowledging local-land possibilities.
- **Quote:** “Geographically, the problem is an infested earth. Note that in 6:5-13, the earth (hāʾāreṣ) is mentioned eight times. Thus the description has all the appearances of a universal condition rather than a local one. … the reference in 7:3 to the animals of kol-hāʾāreṣ argues for an understanding of ʿereṣ elsewhere in the Flood narrative as ‘earth’ … Yet, verses such as Gen. 13:9, 15 show that even in Genesis kol-hāʾāreṣ refers to the whole land.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 39–40; Gen 6:5–13; 7:3
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[flood-universality]]

### C-V1R4-03 | yēṣer: man the potter of evil thoughts
- **Claim:** “Scheme” (*yēṣer*) echoes God “forming” man/animals (2:7, 19); now man fashions his own thoughts—what God forms is beautiful; what man forms is repulsive—and the condition is chronic.
- **Quote:** “scheme, Heb. yēṣer (or, ‘imagination, desire’), is a nominal form of the word used in 2:7, 19 to describe the ‘formation’ of man and animal from the soil. There God was the potter, fashioning man. Now man himself has become the potter, fashioning his thoughts. What God forms is beautiful; what man forms is repulsive. … this kind of malaise is a chronic condition, not just a spasmodic lapse.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 42–42; Gen 6:5 (cf. 8:21)
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[sin]], [[noah]]

### C-V1R4-04 | Gilgamesh/Atrahasis lack moral flood motivation
- **Claim:** Against Gilgamesh and Atrahasis, Genesis opens with clear moral motivation. Gilgamesh’s closest parallel is vague (“when their heart led the great gods to produce the flood”); Ea later rebukes Enlil as “unreasoning.” Atrahasis sends flood because human noise disturbs Enlil’s sleep (overpopulation), not moral rebellion—gods are not necessarily morally superior to humans.
- **Quote:** “It is important to observe that right at the beginning there is a clear-cut moral motivation behind sending the Flood. The Gilgamesh Epic … lacks such a parallel here. … According to a related flood story, the Atrahasis Epic, … Enlil starts to suffer from insomnia. … Finally a flood is sent… To call this noise moral turbulence … reads into the text far too much. The problem is simply that there are too many people, with the result that there is too much noise. … in a system of thought where the gods are not necessarily morally superior to human beings … there is no recording of the fact that man is to be drowned because he is a rebel and a sinner.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 44–46; Gen 6:5; Gilgamesh XI; Atrahasis
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[genesis-ancient-near-east]], [[sin]], [[flood-universality]]

### C-V1R4-05 | Divine regret / pain; God not Impassible Absolute alone
- **Claim:** Yahweh is grieved with pain in his heart—echoing Eve’s and Adam’s pain (3:16–17)—sourced in regret over fallen humanity and the necessity of judgment. Hamilton refuses to dismiss this as empty anthropopathism; OT God feels pain, chagrin, remorse.
- **Quote:** “Viewing the debacle man has fomented, God is grieved, even to the point of experiencing pain in his heart. … verses like this remind us that the God of the OT is not beyond the capability of feeling pain, chagrin, and remorse. To call him the Impassible Absolute is but part of the truth.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 48–48; Gen 6:6
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[sin]]

### C-V1R4-06 | God “repents” (nḥm): changeability with unchangeability
- **Claim:** Niphal *nḥm* often has God as subject; most instances concern possible change of future plan, not past acts—but Gen 6 forces room for both divine unchangeability and changeability. LXX avoids “repent” verbs here.
- **Quote:** “Here we are introduced to the idea of God repenting! … only a few passages that speak of God’s repentance refer to God repenting over something already done. The vast majority … have to do with his possible change of will concerning a future plan of action. … Still, the fact that the OT affirms that God does repent, even over a fait accompli, forces us to make room in our theology for the concepts of both the unchangeability of God and his changeability.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 50–56; Gen 6:6–7
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]]

### C-V1R4-07 | mḥh: erase by washing; judgment by drowning
- **Claim:** The verb for eliminating man (*mḥh*) means “erase by washing”; God erases sinners by drowning them, as elsewhere he “washes away” sins positively.
- **Quote:** “The root in question (mḥh) means ‘to erase by washing.’ … In a positive sense the verb is used in the idiom, ‘the washing away of sins’ … God not only erases sins, but he erases sinners—he judges them by drowning them.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 58–60; Gen 6:7
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[sin]], [[flood-universality]]

### C-V1R4-08 | Noah finds (not wins) favor; grace not works
- **Claim:** Prefer “finding” favor to “winning” favor: finding favor denotes no moral quality securing election; if *ḥēn* = grace, grace is found/received, not won. No causal line forced from v. 8 to v. 9 character description.
- **Quote:** “Most translations … have Noah ‘finding’ favor with Yahweh. A few (e.g., NEB) have Noah ‘winning’ favor… The former denotes no moral quality on the part of the person who is designated as having found favor. On these grounds Noah’s election would be just that… If we translate Heb. ḥēn as ‘grace’ instead of ‘favor,’ then further support for ‘finding’ is available. Grace is found or received, not won.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 64–66; Gen 6:8–9
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[noah]], [[sin]]

### C-V1R4-09 | Toledot 6:9–10: preview then Noah-focus, not two J/P intros
- **Claim:** Against source critics assigning two Flood introductions (6:5–8 J; 6:9–11 P), Hamilton reads 6:5–8 as preview with Yahweh as major actor, then 6:9–11 shifts emphasis to Noah and earth; order reverses wickedness→exemption then character→corruption.
- **Quote:** “The source critics, who assign such titles to P, suggest that there are here two introductions to the Flood story: 6:5-8 (J) and 6:9-11 (P). It seems more accurate to designate 6:5-8 as a preview to the whole story… In 6:9-11 the emphasis shifts to Noah and the earth as the major participants in the drama.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 70–72; Gen 6:5–11
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[toledot]], [[documentary-hypothesis]], [[noah]]

### C-V1R4-10 | Noah: ṣaddîq / tāmîm / walks with God; habitual righteousness
- **Claim:** Noah is righteous, blameless among contemporaries, walks with God—ten Hebrew words, tenth generation from Adam. *Tāmîm* = free from defect / wholesome, not sinless. *Ṣaddîq* implies habitual righteousness (no “occasional” righteous form).
- **Quote:** “Noah was a righteous person. Among his contemporaries he was blameless. With God Noah walked. These three sentences are only ten words in Hebrew. … Of course, Noah was not ‘free from defect.’ He was tāmȋm, but not sinless. … With ṣdq, ‘righteous,’ the only possibility is the one we have here—ṣaddȋq, that is, one who is habitually righteous.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 76–78; Gen 6:9
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[noah]], [[sin]]

### C-V1R4-11 | šāḥaṯ: earth ruined; God ruins what is self-destroying
- **Claim:** Same root describes earth’s corruption and God’s destruction—God destroys what is virtually self-destroyed already (cf. spoiled clay, Jer 18:4). Narrator and God agree the earth is irremediably polluted; “God saw… and behold” may mark surprise.
- **Quote:** “To capture this consistency of word choice we may render… ‘gone to ruin was the earth… all flesh had ruined its way…. I will ruin them.’ … God’s decision is to destroy what is virtually self-destroyed or self-destroying already. … Both are in agreement that the earth is polluted and in an irremediable situation.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 99–103; Gen 6:11–13
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[sin]], [[flood-universality]]

### C-V1R4-12 | ḥāmās / “all flesh”: condensation of Gen 3–6:4
- **Claim:** 6:11–12 condense narratives from 3:1 to 6:4; *ḥāmās* (lawlessness/violence) permeates Cain and Lamech stories. “All flesh” in Flood context is all-inclusive (humans and animals), not humans only.
- **Quote:** “In a sense w. 11-12 are a condensation of the narratives extending from Gen. 3:1 to 6:4. … the earth was full of lawlessness (ḥāmās…). … it is most likely all-inclusive in 6:12.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 105–107; Gen 6:11–12
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[sin]], [[flood-universality]]

### C-V1R4-13 | Ark (tēḇâ): Moses parallel; dimensions logical vs Gilgamesh cube
- **Claim:** *Tēḇâ* only in Flood and Exod 2 (Moses’ basket)—two figures saved from drowning in an “ark.” Dimensions ~440×73×44 ft (~43,000 tons displacement) are “completely logical” for a seagoing vessel, vs Utnapishtim’s perfect 120-cubit cube; large enough for animals (~95,700 sq ft deck).
- **Quote:** “two remarkable persons in Scripture are saved from drowning by being placed in an ‘ark.’ … Translating the cubit measurement into feet, we have a vessel that is 440 feet long, 73 feet wide, 44 feet high… the dimensions of Noah’s vessel are completely logical… Compare these dimensions with those of Utnapishtim’s boat … which is a perfect cube of 120 cubits.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 164–174; Gen 6:14–16
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[noah]], [[genesis-ancient-near-east]]

### C-V1R4-14 | Compartments not reed boat; ṣōhar as pitched roof
- **Claim:** Retain MT *qinnîm* (nests/compartments) against reed emendation (vs Atrahasis reed boat / Moses’ papyrus). *Ṣōhar* better “pitched/vaulted roof” than window (8:6 uses *ḥallôn*); flat *gag* would be unsuitable in a downpour.
- **Quote:** “The acceptance of the MT supports the concept that Noah’s ark was not a reed boat, but a large, complicated, and seaworthy vessel. … We suggest that ṣōhar was used because it refers to a pitched or vaulted roof.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 168–180; Gen 6:14–16
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[noah]], [[genesis-ancient-near-east]]

### C-V1R4-15 | Covenant announced before Flood (6:18); grace precedes wrath
- **Claim:** Covenant with Noah is announced before the Flood, not ad hoc after waters recede; sequence grace-then-indignation already seen with Adam/Eve clothing and Cain’s mark.
- **Quote:** “This announcement of the covenant, even before the Flood commences, is interesting. It shows us that God’s covenant with Noah in ch. 9 is no ad hoc arrangement, hatched in God’s mind once the floodwaters had disappeared. … Before God banished Adam and Eve from the garden he clothed them. Before he exiled Cain he placed a mark on him… And here God announces his covenant even before he sends his flood.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 186–188; Gen 6:18; 9
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[noah]], [[covenant]]

### C-V1R4-16 | Silent Noah; four divine speeches; implements without dialogue
- **Claim:** Flood narrative has four divine speeches; Noah nowhere speaks until “cursed be Canaan” (9:25). God discloses plans; Noah implements—no Abraham-like protest.
- **Quote:** “The Flood narrative has four divine speeches (6:13-21; 7:1-4; 8:15-17; 9:1-17… Interestingly, nowhere does Noah speak. As a matter of fact, his first recorded words in Scripture are ‘cursed be Canaan’ (9:25)! … This narrative has no hint of any dialogue. God speaks. Noah implements.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 160–160; Gen 6–9
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[noah]]

### C-V1R4-17 | One pair vs seven pairs: no J/P contradiction
- **Claim:** 6:19–20 *šenayim* is collective “pairs”; 7:2–3 specifies seven pairs of clean and one pair of unclean—preliminary then expanded instructions, not mutually exclusive P/J numbers. Text avoids *ṭāmēʾ*, saying “not clean”; unclean animals also objects of compassion.
- **Quote:** “most commentators have precipitately assumed a contradiction between the ‘one pair’ (P) and ‘seven pairs’ (J, 7:2-3)… we would suggest that these numbers are not mutually exclusive. … Gen. 6:19-20 is the general statement. … Specifically the animal population is to consist of seven pairs of clean and one pair of unclean. … Yet these unclean animals are spared from drowning. They are as much an object of Yahweh’s compassion as is Noah himself.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 192–270; Gen 6:19–20; 7:2–3, 8–9
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[noah]], [[documentary-hypothesis]]

### C-V1R4-18 | YHWH / ʾĕlōhîm shifts: thematic participants, not J vs P
- **Claim:** Name alternation is not proof of two Flood sources. Hamilton (with Cassuto-type reasoning) explains: general *ʾĕlōhîm* for world inundation; *YHWH* where deity is thematic participant; nonthematic sections use *ʾĕlōhîm* even inside a “Yahweh” unit (e.g. 7:9).
- **Quote:** “Those who perceive a doublet in Gen. 6-9 appeal to this phenomenon to support their case. … This interpretation of the two names for deity is open to serious challenge. … normally Gen. 6-9 uses the more general ’ĕlōhîm (since it is the world that is inundated), and that YHWH occurs only where there is a special reason for it. … it is also evident that in those places where deity is thematic in a given paragraph YHWH is used.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 251–254, 285–285; Gen 6–9; 7:1–10
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[documentary-hypothesis]], [[noah]]

### C-V1R4-19 | 7:1: God chooses Noah; ṣaddîq functional, not works-merit recognition
- **Claim:** “I have seen you, a righteous person” is prospective/choice language (cf. 1 Sam 16:1), not “I found that you are righteous” by works after ark-building. Righteousness explanation is Yahweh’s purpose/choice of representative, not merit.
- **Quote:** “Translations that render the second half of the verse ‘for I have found that you are righteous’ are wide of the mark. Such a translation would give the (false) impression that Noah’s obedience in building the ark is the immediate reason for his salvation, and thus produce a works-righteousness emphasis. … The point made by 7:1 is that the explanation for Noah’s righteousness is not merit, but rather the purpose of Yahweh. God has chosen Noah as the suitable representative of the human race… Thus ṣaddîq has a functional nuance in 7:1.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 257–260; Gen 7:1
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[noah]], [[sin]]

### C-V1R4-20 | Temporal architecture: 7-40-150-40-7; solar year Flood
- **Claim:** Plot uses numbered periods (7, 40, 150, 40, 7) and calendar dates from 2/17/Noah 600 to 2/27/Noah 601—twelve lunar months + eleven days equating lunar to solar year; Flood lasts one solar year.
- **Quote:** “Note how the ‘seven days’ motif surfaces again… 7 days… 40 days… 150 days… 40 days… 7 days… The Flood ‘lasted twelve months and eleven days, the exact period required to equate the year of twelve lunar months, 354 days, with the solar year of 365 days.’ The Flood lasted one solar year.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 291–304, 627–635; Gen 7–8
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[noah]], [[flood-universality]]

### C-V1R4-21 | Flood un-creates: waters above/below; not Enuma elish creation
- **Claim:** Two water sources (abyss springs + sky floodgates) recall 1:6–7; Flood returns earth to pre-creation “waters.” *Bāqaʿ* of *tehôm* is not mythical Tiamat-splitting; themes reverse Enuma elish (chaos released vs order by bisection). Confirms Yahweh’s lordship over waters.
- **Quote:** “There is no doubt that the two sources of water are intended to recall the ‘waters above and below’ of 1:6-7. The Flood un-creates, and returns the earth to a pre-creation period when there was only ‘waters.’ … Note that in Gen. 7:11 chaos is released by the splitting of tehôm. In Enuma elish the gods attempt to create some kind of order by bisecting Tiamat. In other words, the themes are reversed.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 355–367; Gen 7:11
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[genesis-ancient-near-east]], [[flood-universality]]

### C-V1R4-22 | Forty days rain vs seven days in ANE; no ANE navigators
- **Claim:** Forty days/nights is more reasonable than Gilgamesh/Atrahasis’s seven days/nights. Unlike Utnapishtim/Atrahasis, Noah has no navigational crew; survival is grace/protection of Yahweh, not human skill—though birds and window are implicit navigational practice.
- **Quote:** “Such rain fell for forty days and forty nights, a much more reasonable figure for a flood of this proportion than the relatively brief seven days and seven nights found in both the Gilgamesh and Atrahasis epics. … Noah, unlike Utnapishtim and Atrahasis, does not have navigational personnel aboard… If Noah is to emerge alive from the ark, it will be because of the grace and protecting presence of Yahweh—divine mercy rather than human skill will be the determining factor.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 370–370, 462–462, 590–592; Gen 7–8
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[noah]], [[genesis-ancient-near-east]]

### C-V1R4-23 | Universal death; death as divine penalty; Noah left over by Yahweh
- **Claim:** 7:19–23: highest mountains submerged; all flesh dies. Prefer *mētû* “died” over “drowned” to mark divine penalty (cf. 2:17). Noah survives because *yiššāʾer*—left over by Yahweh; family saved because of Noah.
- **Quote:** “Nowhere does the text say ‘they drowned’… the use of mēṯû, ‘they died,’ … reinforces the idea that the loss of life is a divine penalty… Noah does not survive this catastrophe by his own cunning or strength. He is saved because he is left behind, or left over … by Yahweh. … Noah is saved because of Yahweh. And Noah’s family is saved because of Noah.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 409–475; Gen 7:19–23
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[noah]], [[flood-universality]], [[sin]]

- **Claim:** Against assigning 7:11–16 as P doublet of 7:6–9, Hamilton argues deliberate epic resumption (flood/entry alternation) and chiastic symmetry in 7:5–24; dissecting sources is unproductive.

### C-V1R4-26 | “God remembered Noah”: mercy action, not merit flashback
- **Claim:** Pivot of story is “God remembered Noah”—not Noah’s righteousness, not merely recalling 6:18 covenant words. *Zākar* with God is action toward someone (saving from death), not psychological experience.

### C-V1R4-27 | Wind / rûaḥ and sealed waters: re-creation; no sun-god
- **Claim:** Divine *rûaḥ*/wind over earth echoes 1:2; passive verbs for sealing waters match opening passives—Flood’s start and end are divinely controlled. Absence of sun in drying dissociates biblical end-of-flood from Sumerian sun-god Utu (Ziusudra).
- **Quote:** “One need only recall that Heb. rûaḥ translates as both ‘spirit’ and ‘wind’ in order to decipher here a blatant connection with 1:2. … This fourfold use of a passive form of the verb says as strongly as possible that the Flood is not a freak of nature. Both its commencement and completion are divinely ordained… Note that the sun plays no role in the drying up of the waters, though in the pagan myths of castastrophe the sun plays a primary role”

### C-V1R4-28 | Landing: mountains of Ararat / Urartu, not “Mt. Ararat”; vs Nisir
- **Claim:** Text says *hārê ʾarārāṭ*—one of the mountains of Ararat (Urartu/Armenia), not “Mt. Ararat.” Gilgamesh lands on Mt. Nisir (~9000 ft, farther SE); Ararat region higher. Wordplay: ark *tānaḥ* / Noah *nōaḥ*.

### C-V1R4-29 | Birds: navigational practice; raven-then-dove vs Gilgamesh; late ANE parallel
- **Claim:** Bird-sending reflects actual navigation (not mere folklore). Biblical order raven then dove is more realistic than Gilgamesh dove→swallow→raven. Surviving bird parallel in Gilgamesh XI copies is post-750 BC; earlier Sumerian flood lacks birds—so “most telling parallel” postdates biblical account. Noah still awaits divine command to disembark.
- **Quote:** “Noah’s releasing of the birds should be seen as a reflection of actual navigational practice, rather than as a bit of folkloristic coloring. … The biblical sequence has more of the ring of truth about it. … ‘the only surviving testimony to the most telling parallel [between the OT and Mesopotamian Flood myths] happens to be later than the Biblical account.’”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 583–619; Gen 8:6–12

### C-V1R4-30 | ḥāraḇ then yāḇaš: creation resurfacing, not J/P doublet
- **Claim:** 8:13–14 dual “dry” reports use different verbs (*ḥāraḇ* free of moisture; *yāḇaš* complete dryness / dry land of Gen 1)—logical sequence and dual perspective (Noah’s observation vs objective report), not needless J/P repetition.
- **Quote:** “Is this needless repetition, or evidence of the presence of J and P? Perhaps there is another explanation. … In v. 13 the verb is ḥāraḇ… In v. 14 it is yāḇaš… Creation, destroyed in the Flood, is now resurfacing. … V. 13 records the drying of the ground from Noah’s observation… V. 14 records the same result, but here it is an objective reporting statement.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 624–635; Gen 8:13–14
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[documentary-hypothesis]], [[flood-universality]]

### C-V1R4-31 | First altar; holocaust; rest-inducing odor; no hungry gods
- **Claim:** Noah’s first post-disembark act is building the first biblical altar and offering whole burnt offerings. *Rēaḥ hannîḥōaḥ* acoustically ties to Noah (*nōaḥ*). Unlike Gilgamesh/Atrahasis, gods do not swarm “like flies” starving after the flood; Yahweh’s soliloquy to himself avoids framing sacrifice as magic manipulation.
- **Quote:** “This is the first reference in the Bible to an altar. … This verse does not mention the motif of God’s craving for food. The lack of this theme is striking when one compares the biblical story with the Gilgamesh Epic and the Atrahasis Epic. In both the Mesopotamian stories the survivor also offers a food sacrifice to the gods, who swarm around it ‘like flies’… Had Noah been the recipient of this information, the story would have opened the door to the possibility that what is involved here is not genuine propitiation but magic”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 702–716; Gen 8:20–21
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[noah]], [[genesis-ancient-near-east]], [[covenant]]

### C-V1R4-32 | 8:21 kî concessive: grace despite enduring evil yēṣer
- **Claim:** If *kî* = “because,” paradox: Flood for human evil, then no more Flood because of human evil. Hamilton prefers concessive “although/even though”: mercy will not give man just deserts; *leqallēl* = treat harshly (Brichto), not merely “designate as accursed.” Seasonal regularity (8:22) is promised grace, not fertility-cult sympathetic magic.
- **Quote:** “Here is the paradox: God inundates the earth because of man’s sinfulness, and subsequently promises never again to destroy the earth because of man’s sinfulness. … Thus this verse functions as a ringing testimony to the mercy of God, who henceforth will not give man his just deserts. The punishable will not be punished. … it denies the dynamics of the fertility cult by stressing that man’s actions for good or evil have no impact on the patterns of the season.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 716–728; Gen 8:21–22
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[sin]], [[covenant]], [[flood-universality]]

- **Claim:** Against reading 9:1–17 as P’s second Flood conclusion parallel to J’s 8:20–22, Hamilton takes 8:20–22 as covenant in incipient form and 9:1–17 as amplification/specification.

We would suggest that 8:20-22 is the announcement of God’s post-Deluge covenant in incipient form. Then 9:1-17 would be seen as an amplification and specification of this anticipatory note.”

### C-V1R4-34 | Noah as second Adam; vs Atrahasis population control
- **Claim:** “Be fruitful… fill the earth” transports reader to Gen 1; Noah is second Adam. Atrahasis ends with birth control (barren women, demon snatching babies, celibate priestesses)—opposite of Genesis; Gen 9:1ff looks like conscious rejection of Atrahasis.
- **Quote:** “Noah is a second Adam. What God told Adam he now tells Noah. … Thus the Atrahasis Epic concludes on a note exactly the opposite of the biblical story. It says that overpopulation is the earth’s primary problem… ‘Viewed in this light, Gen. 9: 1ff looks like a conscious rejection of the Atrahasis Epic.’”

### C-V1R4-35 | Post-Flood discontinuity: meat permitted; blood & murder Noachian
- **Claim:** Continuity with Gen 1 (fruitfulness) but discontinuity: animals now food under dread; pattern of permission + one prohibition like 2:16–17. Blood consumption ban is first of many, without ANE parallel—Noachian not only Sinaitic. Image of God still present grounds capital sanction; vv. 5–6 allow God or man to exact blood for murder (“by man” preferred).
- **Quote:** “Human exploitation of animal life is here set within the context of a post-Flood, deteriorated situation. … Eating blood and taking life are Noachian commandments, not Sinaitic ones. … There is no evidence here that sin has effaced the divine image. … this verse has become the scriptural locus classicus for capital punishment. … The penalty for shedding blood may be exacted either by God (v. 5) or by man (v. 6).”

### C-V1R4-36 | Unilateral Noachian covenant; animals included; Flood unique
- **Claim:** God “establishes/erects” (*qûm* Hiphil) covenant with Noah, descendants, and every living creature—unilateral; animals’ inclusion proves validity does not depend on recipient acceptance. Sequence (human obligations 1–7 before “I will” 8–17) preserves unilaterality: no “you shall” after “I will.” Covenant content: never again all flesh cut off by floodwaters.
- **Quote:** “That the covenant is extended to animals is certain proof that the validity of this covenant is not dependent upon acceptance by the recipient of the covenant promise. Animals do not accept a covenant. … The thrust of this covenant is that the Flood is unique. … The present order preserves the emphasis on the unilaterality of the post-Flood situation. No ‘you shall’ follows ‘I will.’”

### C-V1R4-37 | Rainbow (qešet): warrior bow reinterpreted as peace sign for God
- **Claim:** *Qešet* is both rainbow and weapon; ANE iconography and OT Yahweh-as-warrior use bow lethally. Gen 9 radically reinterprets: bow becomes peace symbol—cessation of hostilities. Sign is for God’s remembering (anthropomorphism even in “P”), like Passover blood God “sees.” Rejects Yamm-conquest myth reading and sexual-symbol overreadings as primary.
- **Quote:** “in what is nothing less than a radical reinterpretation of divine power, the bow ceases to function as a symbol of combat and is now a symbol of peace and well-being. … It is surprising, perhaps, to read that the sign is for God’s benefit, not for man’s. When he sees it, he will remember the promise he made to Noah. … what are we to make of this most conspicuous anthropomorphism right in the middle of a pericope that all source critics attribute to P?”

### C-V1R4-39 | Ham’s sin: seeing nakedness + telling; not castration/incest
- **Claim:** Section titled by nakedness not drunkenness. Reject midrashic castration/sodomy and Basset’s incest-with-mother reading (cannot square with brothers covering father). Ham’s sin: observing genitalia and failing to cover, then publicizing to brothers—dishonoring father, fomenting fraternal strife.

### C-V1R4-40 | Curse on Canaan (not Ham): optative request, not magic
- **Claim:** Noah’s first words: “Cursed be Canaan.” Prefer optative over immediately effective decree (jussives follow; appeal to God in v. 27 lifts out of potent magic). Why Canaan not Ham remains unexplained; several proposals listed without adjudication. Blessing directed to Yahweh (Shem’s God) not Shem—subordinates human actors.
- **Quote:** “Here the optative thrust seems preferable… That Noah appeals to God in v. 27 also lifts the words of Noah out of the area of potent magic and into the realm of request. … A perusal of these attempts to unravel a mystery makes clear that we do not know why the son bears the consequences of the father’s improprieties. … by directing the blessing to Yahweh instead of to Shem, the narrator subordinates the human actors to the divine actor.”

- **Claim:** Pun *yapte ʾĕlōhîm leyepet*. Japheth = generally Gentiles / Anatolian-Aegean Indo-European peoples (sometimes tied to Sea Peoples). ### C-V1R4-42 | NT: 1 Pet 3 / 2 Pet 2 / Matt–Luke / Heb 11 on Flood
- **Claim:** (1) 2 Pet 2:5: Noah + Lot as spared righteous vs judged contemporaries—warning to false teachers. (2) 1 Pet 3:20–21: typological baptism; prefer local *di’ hýdatos* “through water” (got soaked, didn’t drown) over instrumental “by water,” so type is passage through death into salvation, not Peter twisting Genesis. ## H. THE TABLE OF NATIONS (10:1–32)

### C-V1R4-43 | Table structure: chiastic whole; against J/P composite
- **Claim:** Segmented genealogy of Noah’s three sons fulfills 9:1 blessing (all three multiply; Ham/Canaan productive despite curse). Source split (P ~1–7, 20, 22–23, 31–32; J ~8–19, 21, 24–30) overstates disjointedness. Whole shows chiastic summary: intro order Shem–Ham–Japheth reversed in body Japheth–Ham–Shem; each unit starts with patriarch and ends with families/languages/lands/nations; v. 32 inclusio with v. 1.
- **Quote:** “Yet the chapter, read as a whole, does not appear disjointed. Indeed, the entire genealogy provides an example of chiastic summary that streamlines the parts into a whole: (1) Noah’s sons are listed in the opening verse in this order: Shem, Ham, and Japheth; yet in the paragraphs that follow this order is reversed… (3) the last verse of the chapter (v. 32) forms an inclusio with the chapter’s first verse.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1092–1098; Gen 10:1–32
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[toledot]], [[documentary-hypothesis]], [[noah]]

### C-V1R4-44 | Toledot formula variation Qal/Niphal/“sons of”
- **Claim:** Ch. 10 *tôleḏôṯ* uses Qal *yālaḏ* (and one Niphal in v. 1) vs Gen 5’s Hiphil; “fathered” falls in J-attributed sections and “the sons of” in P-attributed—Hamilton reports the source mapping while treating the chapter as a literary whole.
- **Quote:** “Unlike Gen. 5, which uses the Hiphil of yālaḏ (imperfect) when speaking of ‘fathering,’ ch. 10 uses consistently the Qal of yālaḏ … except for v. 1, which provides the only use of the Niphal of yālaḏ in the chapter. Elsewhere in the chapter the formula is simply: ‘the sons of’… Each instance of ‘fathered’ falls within the section of the chapter attributed to J, and ‘the sons of’ is to be found in the P sections of the chapter.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1098–1098; Gen 10
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[toledot]], [[documentary-hypothesis]]

### C-V1R4-45 | Ecumene: one world civilization; odd links intentional
- **Claim:** Gen 11:1 summarizes ch. 10 as *kol-hāʾāreṣ*—the known world’s ecumene. Unexpected links (Nimrod from Cush; Hamitic Canaan) testify to ecumenic beginnings: internationalism precedes nationalism.
- **Quote:** “Gen. 11:1 summarizes the findings of Gen. 10 in two Hebrew words: kol-hā’āreṣ, literally, ‘all the earth.’ This reference to the whole (known) world is what we would call the ecumene… such links testify to the ecumenic nature of civilization’s beginnings. Internationalism precedes nationalism and provincialism.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1100–1100; Gen 10; 11:1
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[genesis-ancient-near-east]]

### C-V1R4-46 | Japhethites: maritime peoples N/NW of Israel
- **Claim:** Japheth’s seven sons + seven grandsons map to Anatolian/Aegean/Iranian groups (Gomer/Cimmerians, Magog/Gyges-Lydia, Madai/Medes, Javan/Ionia, Tubal, Meshech, Tiras/Etruscans, etc.). Primarily maritime nations north/northeast/northwest of Israel; Philistines excluded for geography. Uses *gôy* not *ʿam*—less personal conglomerates.
- **Quote:** “It is clear that the descendants of Japheth are primarily, if not exclusively, ethnic groups that represent maritime nations… All the nations or peoples enumerated in vv. 1-5 are located either north, northeast, or northwest of Israel… Speiser has observed that gôy, ‘nation,’ is consistently used in this chapter, but ʽam, ‘people,’ never is.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1102–1126; Gen 10:1–5
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[noah]]

### C-V1R4-47 | Canaan as Hamite: sociocultural (city/kingdom), not race genetics
- **Claim:** Canaan under Ham surprises if Canaanites are “as Semitic as the Hebrews.” Possible reasons: reflects 9:20–27 curse; geographic proximity; or—preferred—sociocultural: sedentary city civilization like Egypt/Babylon (*mamlākâ*, *ʿîr* appear only in this unit).
- **Quote:** “Possibly Canaan is linked with the likes of Egypt and Babylon in this unit (and all under the rubric of Hamites) because like them Canaan was, from the Bible’s perspective, a sedentary population, dwelling in cities ‘which are great and walled up to heaven’ (Deut. 1:28). Thus the reason for listing Canaan as Hamitic is not personal or geographical but sociocultural.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1202–1202; Gen 10:6–20
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[noah]], [[sin]]

### C-V1R4-48 | Nimrod: hunter-king; Mesopotamian cities; Yahweh’s grace
- **Claim:** Nimrod gets more comment than anyone else—first mighty on earth, hero of the chase “by Yahweh’s grace.” Identification options: Ninurta; Tukulti-Ninurta I; Amenhotep III—Hamilton reports without sole adjudication; Mic 5:5 links “land of Nimrod” with Assyria. Kingdom: Babylon, Erech, Accad, and Calneh (or “all of them” emendation) in Shinar; Asshur/Nineveh complex follows. Etymology often tied to *mārad* “rebel” (Haggadah); Dahood: “panther of Hadd.”
- **Quote:** “Nimrod receives more comment than anyone else in ch. 10. … That Nimrod is styled as the hero of the chase points both to the martial prowess of this individual against other nations and to the hunting of wild game. This power, however, is a gift of God’s grace. … Mic. 5:5 (Eng. 6), with its ‘land of Nimrod’ as a synonymous variant of Assyria, establishes Nimrod as a territory to the east of Palestine.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1210–1226; Gen 10:8–12
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[genesis-ancient-near-east]], [[noah]]

### C-V1R4-49 | Shemites last for climax; Eber pivotal; Peleg “divided”
- **Claim:** Shem last for climactic effect (Abraham’s line); Shem is Japheth’s older brother despite final position. Eber highlighted though three generations down—Eberites pivotal. Peleg: “in his time the earth was divided”—most likely anticipates Babel dispersal (not only canal-building or Pelegite/Joktanite split). Joktan’s thirteen sons map Arabian groups; territory Mesha to Sephar.
- **Quote:** “The Shemites are the last in this table because they are the most crucial, the line from which Abraham will emerge. Thus, their placement is for climactic effect. … it is not just Shemites that are pivotal, but the Eberites in particular. … Or, more likely, does this datum presage the Tower of Babel story in which men were driven away, divided from each other, and forced to settle elsewhere?”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1306–1320; Gen 10:21–30
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[toledot]], [[noah]]

### C-V1R4-50 | Table theology: common origin, one God, Israel within world
- **Claim:** Table unique in ANE literature (no Egyptian/cuneiform parallel). Theological value: one world under one God; Israel chosen yet ch. 10 emphasizes commonality more than uniqueness—all humanity shares origin and thus nobility/value. Cf. Acts 17:26.
- **Quote:** “It is not without interest that such a table of nations is unique to OT literature. Neither the hieroglyphic nor the cuneiform worlds produced a parallel document. The theological value of the Table is that it affirms Israel as part of one world governed by one God. … Gen. 10 emphasizes Israel’s commonality with the other nations more than it does its uniqueness. What the chapter affirms is that all of humanity, in spite of geographical and linguistic differences, share a common origin. And in this common origin is to be found humanity’s nobility and inherent value.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1332–1332; Gen 10:32
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[noah]], [[covenant]]

### C-V1R4-51 | Ch. 10 before 11: blessing then judgment; effect before cause
- **Claim:** Table (effect) precedes Babel (cause). Not best explained as P/J doublet alone. Present order: ch. 10 fills 9:1 fruitfulness/blessing; ch. 11 adds judgment—dispersal reflects both grace and displeasure (cf. Cain). Alternately, placing Babel next to patriarchal solution (ch. 12) juxtaposes problem and Abrahamic remedy; inserting ch. 10 between would blunt that.
- **Quote:** “The significance of its present position, however, is that the Table fills out and fulfills the divine promise and imperative in 9:1, ‘be abundantly fruitful.’ Thus the dispersal of humanity throughout the world reflects both God’s blessing (ch. 10) and his displeasure (ch. 11)… By placing the Tower of Babel incident just prior to the patriarchal stories… problem (ch. 11) and solution (ch. 12) are brought into immediate juxtaposition, and the forcefulness of this structural move would have been lost had ch. 10 intervened between the two.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1334–1346; Gen 10–12
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[toledot]], [[covenant]], [[documentary-hypothesis]]

### C-V1R4-52 | NT: Luke 10 seventy(-two) and Gen 10 nations
- **Claim:** Luke alone records sending of seventy/seventy-two; MS evidence split. MT has seventy nations, LXX seventy-two. Most likely Jesus reflects Gen 10’s seventy nations—sending representatives into all known nations; world he created he must redeem.
- **Quote:** “the most likely explanation is that Jesus is here reflecting Gen. 10 with its listing of the seventy nations of the then known world. Taken in this way, the number signifies that Jesus is sending his representatives into all the known nations of their day. The world he created he must also redeem.”
- **Locus:** slice ll. 1355–1362; Gen 10 // Luke 10:1
- **Targets:** [[hamilton-genesis-1-17-nicot]], [[victor-hamilton]], [[genesis]], [[noah]]
